Lewiston.metaTitle: Wildlife Removal in Lewiston, ME | Androscoggin County Pros
Lewiston.metaDescription: Rats, bats, raccoons and skunks in Lewiston, ME. Mill-era housing near Lisbon Street and the Androscoggin River, with same-day service from our crew — call us today.
Lewiston.housing_era: Lewiston is defined by mill-era brick tenements and triple-deckers built for textile workers, dense wood-frame multifamily housing near downtown, and later single-family neighborhoods on the outer streets. Many older buildings share walls, chimneys and rooflines that wildlife can travel between.
Lewiston.geographic_features: Androscoggin River (mill-dammed river through the twin cities), Lewiston Falls and the Great Falls area (river gorge below downtown), Kennedy Park area waterways and canals (historic mill canals through downtown), Lake Auburn drainage to the north (wooded corridor into the city edge)

Lewiston.wildlife_intro:
Lewiston gives our crew more rat and bat work than almost anywhere else in this part of Maine, and the reason is the housing itself. The mill-era triple-deckers and brick tenements near Lisbon Street and downtown have old chimneys, shared rooflines and worn soffits that bats slip into in summer and raccoons test all winter. Norway rats are a steady problem around older commercial blocks, dumpsters and the river and canal corridors, especially where food waste and harborage sit close together. Skunks den under porches and sheds, and gray squirrels work the mature street trees into attics.

Winters here are long and hard, so by late fall animals are looking for warm wall voids and chimneys, and spring brings young raccoons and skunks under decks. Most Lewiston jobs start with a careful inspection of the whole roofline and foundation, because sealing one hole in a connected older building rarely holds on its own. Our work is done by an MDIFW-certified Animal Damage Control agent, with exclusion and sealing first and trapping only where it is needed.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Lewiston?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Why are rats such a problem in Lewiston's older neighborhoods?
faqs.a: Older multifamily housing, shared basements and alleys, restaurant and dumpster waste, and the river and canal corridors give Norway rats food, water and hidden travel routes in a small area. Killing rats without sealing entry points and tightening waste storage does not last, so we pair removal with exclusion and practical sanitation steps for the building.

Auburn.wildlife_intro:
Auburn sits across the Androscoggin River from Lewiston but has a more spread-out feel, and the wildlife calls follow that pattern. Bats turn up in older downtown homes and in barns and outbuildings on the rural edges, raccoons work chimneys and trash in New Auburn and East Auburn, and gray squirrels are constant where mature trees overhang rooflines. Skunks den under porches and sheds, and properties near Lake Auburn and the Little Androscoggin River also see beaver activity in culverts and wet edges that can flood yards and camp roads.

Severe winter weather pushes animals into attics and crawl spaces by late fall, while spring and early summer bring litters in chimneys and under decks. Lake homes that sit quiet in winter sometimes open in spring to bat droppings or a raccoon that moved in through a damaged vent. We inspect the roofline, chimney and foundation together, seal what we find, and use one-way exits for bats so the colony leaves on its own without being handled.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: I found bats in my Auburn attic — can they just be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are handled by exclusion only. We find the entry points, fit one-way devices so bats can leave but not return, then seal the building once it is clear. That work is timed carefully: exclusion from unoccupied buildings is not done in June and July under Maine rules, and wider timing guidance from MDIFW helps protect flightless pups, so an inspection first tells us the right window.

Lisbon.wildlife_intro:
Lisbon's calls come mostly from Lisbon Falls and the older homes along the Androscoggin and Sabattus rivers. Gray squirrels and bats use the older chimneys and eaves in the mill village, raccoons den in chimneys and under porches, and skunks are a familiar problem under sheds and steps in spring. The river corridors keep wildlife close: animals follow the wooded banks at night and cut through yards looking for bird seed, pet food and unsecured trash, and beavers occasionally block culverts on the smaller streams.

A typical job here is an attic inspection after scratching is heard overhead, followed by sealing and a one-way exit where squirrels or bats are involved. Winter makes the pattern sharper, because a warm attic in a Lisbon Falls home stands out when the river valley is well below freezing. In spring we get the other half of the work: young animals under decks, skunks spraying near foundations, and homeowners opening sheds and camps to find something moved in over winter.

faqs.q: Are the snakes I see near the Sabattus River dangerous?
faqs.a: No. Maine has no venomous snakes, and the snakes most often seen near Lisbon's rivers are harmless garter snakes and milk snakes that eat rodents and frogs. Our crew can identify a snake from a photo taken at a distance, reassure you about the species, and, if one is inside a home, remove it without harming it.

Poland.wildlife_intro:
Poland is lake and camp country, and that shapes almost every call we take here. Seasonal camps around Range Pond and Tripp Lake sit empty for months, and raccoons, bats and red and gray squirrels move into quiet attics, chimneys and crawl spaces while no one is there to notice. Skunks den under camp steps and porches, and the wooded shorelines give animals cover right up to the foundation. Poland Spring and the older farmhouses inland add the usual pattern of bats in old chimneys and squirrels in eaves.

Spring opening is our busiest moment in Poland: owners arrive to droppings, chewed screens or a skunk smell under the camp, and the work is to clear the building and seal it before summer use. Fall is the prevention season, when we close gaps before winter denning. Because many camps are unoccupied for long stretches, we pay special attention to bat timing rules and to sealing that will hold through snow load and ice without anyone checking on the building.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. faqs.q: We only use our Poland camp in summer — how do we keep animals out over winter?
faqs.a: The best protection is a fall sealing visit before you close up: cap the chimney, screen vents, close soffit and foundation gaps, and remove food and bird seed from inside. Animals choose quiet camps precisely because no one interrupts them. If something is already inside in spring, call us before staying overnight so we can check for bats or a raccoon family first.

Turner.housing_era: Turner is an agricultural town of older farmhouses, barns and orchard properties, with village homes in Turner Center and Turner Village and newer houses along the main roads. Barns, silos and old farmhouse chimneys give bats, raccoons and pigeons ready shelter.

Turner.wildlife_intro:
Turner is farm country, and the wildlife work here looks different from the mill towns downriver. Groundhogs burrow along field edges, gardens and barn foundations, skunks den under porches and outbuildings, and raccoons raid sweet corn, trash and chicken feed as readily as they den in chimneys. Bats are common in older farmhouses and barns, gray squirrels work the big shade trees around village homes, and much of what homeowners blame on moles in spring is actually voles that tunneled under the snow, with hairy-tailed moles adding their own ridges in lawns and pastures.

Winter drives the indoor work: a heated farmhouse attic is prime shelter when fields are snow-covered, and we hear scratching calls from Turner Center and North Turner through the cold months. Summer shifts the work outdoors to groundhog burrows, skunk dens and beaver trouble on farm streams. Our crew focuses on exclusion around the house and barn, protecting feed and waste storage, and handling each species in the way Maine rules allow rather than with one approach for everything.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Turner?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Is the tunneling in my Turner lawn from moles or something else?
faqs.a: Often it is voles, not moles. Voles tunnel and feed under snow cover and leave surface runs and bark damage that show up at melt, while hairy-tailed moles push up ridged tunnels hunting worms and grubs. Star-nosed moles favor wetter soils near streams. An inspection lets us tell which animal is active so you do not pay to treat the wrong one.

Durham.wildlife_intro:
Durham's large wooded lots and farm properties keep wildlife close to homes all year. Raccoons den in chimneys and barns, skunks move in under porches and sheds, and bats roost in older farmhouse attics and outbuildings along Royalsborough Road and the river frontage. Gray squirrels are steady attic intruders where oaks overhang a roof, and groundhogs work garden edges and field stone walls. With fewer streetlights and larger lots than the twin cities, animals move through Durham yards with little disturbance after dark.

The jobs here tend to be practical and property-wide: seal the farmhouse, screen the barn openings that matter, and deal with the skunk den under the steps before a dog finds it. Severe winters push more animals toward heated buildings, and spring melt reveals vole and mole activity across lawns that sat under deep snow. We work as an MDIFW-certified Animal Damage Control agent, so protected species and rabies-vector animals like skunks and raccoons are handled the way Maine requires.

faqs.q: A skunk is living under our Durham porch — what happens next?

Afterward we screen the porch opening with buried hardware cloth so the next skunk cannot dig back in. Keep dogs away from the area until the den is clear.

Mechanic Falls.wildlife_intro:
Mechanic Falls is a small river village, and most of our work is in the older homes within a short walk of the Little Androscoggin River. Bats find the gaps in older village chimneys and eaves, gray squirrels move from big yard trees into attics, and raccoons and skunks den under the porches and sheds that almost every older home here has. The river corridor brings animals through town at night, and the surrounding farmland adds groundhogs along gardens and stone walls in summer.

Winter is when the attic calls spike, as animals settle into warm spaces above heated rooms, and spring brings skunk activity under steps just as yards thaw. Because the village housing is close together, one unsealed chimney or shed can mean repeat problems for the same street, so we look at the neighboring entry points during an inspection and explain what the whole building needs. The goal is a sealed house that stays quiet through the next winter, not a single animal removed and the hole left open.

faqs.q: We hear scratching in the attic at night in Mechanic Falls — what could it be?

Droppings, entry size and the time you hear it help us narrow it down on inspection. Do not block the hole yourself until we know what is inside, or animals can be trapped in the walls.
